butir.teks: And the goal of unveiling is knowledge of Allah Most High. By it I do not mean the belief that the common person picks up by inheritance or by hearsay, nor the method of polishing speech and disputation in fortifying discourse against the evasions of opponents, as is the goal of the theologian. Rather it is a kind of certainty that is the fruit of a light which Allah Most High casts into the heart of a servant whose inner self has been purified from vile things through spiritual struggle, until he reaches the rank of the faith of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), whose faith, if it were weighed against the faith of all the worlds, would outweigh it (١), as the master of humankind (peace and blessings be upon him) testified for him. So I do not think that what the common person believes and the theologian arranges, who exceeds the common person only in the craft of speech (and for that reason his craft was called kalam), is something that Umar, Uthman, Ali and the rest of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were incapable of, such that Abu Bakr excelled them by the secret that had settled in his heart.

It is astonishing that one should hear such sayings from the Lawgiver (peace and blessings be upon him), then disdain what he hears in agreement with them, and claim that it is among the nonsense of the Sufis and that it is not intelligible. So you should be deliberate in this, for then you would have squandered your capital. Be eager to know that secret which lies outside the merchandise of the jurists and the theologians, and nothing will guide you to it except your eagerness in seeking.

In sum, the noblest of the sciences and their goal is knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is a sea whose farthest depth cannot be reached, and the highest degree that human beings attain in it is the rank of the prophets, then the friends of Allah (awliya'), then those who come after them.

It has been related that the likeness of two of the earlier sages was seen in a mosque, and in the hand of one of them was a scroll on which was written: "If you do everything well, do not think that you have done anything well until you know Allah Most High and know that He is the Cause of causes and the One who brings things into existence."
And in the hand of the other was written: "Before I knew Allah Most High, I would drink and remain thirsty; but when I came to know Him, I was quenched without drinking."

The seventh duty: that he not plunge into a field of knowledge until he has completed the field before it, for the sciences are arranged in a necessary order, and some of them are a path to others. The one granted success is he who observes that order and gradation.

Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 2:121⟧ that is, they do not pass beyond a field until they have mastered it in knowledge and in practice. His aim in every science he pursues should be to rise to what is above it. So he should not judge a science to be corrupt because of disagreement among its people about it, nor because of a mistake by one or a few of them in it, nor because they act contrary to what their knowledge requires. You see groups who abandoned looking into the rational sciences and the juristic sciences, excusing themselves by saying that if these had any basis, those versed in them would have grasped it. The exposure of these fallacies has already been given in the Book Mi'yar al-'Ilm. And you see a group who believe medicine to be invalid because of an error they witnessed from a physician, a group who believed astrology to be sound because of a correct result that happened to one person, and a group who believed it to be invalid because of an error that happened to another.
And all of that is a mistake; rather,

a thing should be known in itself, for it is not the case that every person is able, on his own, to encompass every science. For that reason Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Do not know the truth through men; know the truth and you will know its people."

The eighth duty: that he know the cause by which the noblest sciences are recognised, and that this refers to two things: the first is the nobility of the fruit, and the second is the soundness and strength of the proof. That is like the knowledge of religion and the knowledge of medicine, for the fruit of the one is eternal life and the fruit of the other is perishable life, so the knowledge of religion is nobler.

The same holds for the knowledge of arithmetic and the knowledge of the stars: the knowledge of arithmetic is nobler because of the soundness and strength of its proofs. If arithmetic is compared with medicine, medicine is nobler with regard to its fruit and arithmetic is nobler with regard to its proofs, and attention to the fruit is more fitting. For that reason medicine is nobler, even though most of it rests on conjecture.

From this it becomes clear that the noblest of the sciences is knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His angels, His books, and His messengers, together with knowledge of the path that leads to these sciences. So beware of desiring anything but it, or being eager for anything but it.

The ninth duty: that the learner's aim at present be to adorn his inner self and beautify it with virtue, and in the end to draw near to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and to rise to the company of the Highest Assembly of the angels and those brought near (muqarrabun); and that he not aim by it at leadership, wealth, status, disputing with fools, or boasting before his peers. If this is his aim, he will inevitably seek what is nearest to his aim, and that is the knowledge of the Hereafter. Even so, he ought not look with contempt upon the rest of the sciences, I mean the knowledge of legal opinions and the knowledge of grammar and language that relate to the Book and the Sunna, and the other kinds of sciences that are communal obligations (fard kifaya), which we mentioned in the preliminary and supplementary sections. And do not understand from our excess in praising the knowledge of the Hereafter that we disparage these sciences. Those who take charge of the sciences are like those who take charge of the frontiers, those stationed on them, and the raiders striving in the way of Allah: among them is the fighter, among them the supporter, among them the one who gives them water, and among them the one who guards their mounts and looks after them. None of them is without reward if his aim is to exalt the word of Allah Most High rather than to obtain spoils. So it is with the scholars. Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 58:11⟧ and Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 3:163⟧ And excellence is relative.

Our belittling of money-changers when they are compared with kings does not indicate that they are lowly when they are compared with sweepers. So do not think that whatever falls below the highest rank is worthless; rather, the highest rank belongs to the prophets, then the friends of Allah (awliya'), then the scholars firmly grounded in knowledge, then the righteous according to their varying degrees. In sum, ⟦QS 99:7-8⟧ And whoever seeks Allah Most High by means of knowledge, of whatever kind, it will inevitably benefit him and raise him.

The tenth duty: that he know the relation of the sciences to the goal, so that he prefers the lofty and near over the distant, and the important over the rest. The meaning of the important is what concerns you, and nothing concerns you except your own affair in this world and the Hereafter.

If you cannot combine the delights of this world with the bliss of the Hereafter, as the Qur'an declares and as is attested by what the light of insight offers, which is on a par with direct sight, then the more important is what remains forever and ever. At that point this world becomes a way-station, the body a mount, and deeds a striving toward the goal, and there is no goal except the meeting with Allah Most High, for in it lies all bliss, even though in this world only a few know its worth.

In relation to the happiness of meeting Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and gazing upon His Noble Face (I mean the gazing that the prophets sought and understood, not what first occurs to the understanding of the common people and the theologians), the sciences fall into three levels, which you will grasp by comparison with an example. It is that of a slave whose emancipation and installation in kingship are made contingent on the pilgrimage, and who is told: "If you perform the pilgrimage and complete it, you will reach both emancipation and kingship; and if you set out on the way of the pilgrimage and prepare for it, but a necessary obstacle hinders you on the way, then you will have emancipation and release from the misery of slavery only, without the happiness of kingship." So he has three kinds of occupation.
The first: preparing the means, by buying the she-camel, stitching the waterskin, and readying provisions and the mount.
The second: journeying and leaving the homeland, heading toward the Kaaba, stage after stage.

The third: occupying himself with the rites of the pilgrimage, one pillar after another. Then, after finishing and putting off the state of ihram and performing the farewell circumambulation, he becomes entitled to put himself in the way of kingship and sovereignty. And in each station he has stages, from the beginning of preparing the means to its end,
from the beginning of crossing the deserts to its end, and from the first of the pillars of the pilgrimage to its end.

The nearness to happiness of one who has begun with the pillars of the pilgrimage is not like the nearness of one who is still preparing provisions and mount, nor like the nearness of one who has begun the journey; rather, he is nearer than the latter. So the sciences too are three kinds: a kind that stands in the place of preparing provisions and mount and buying the she-camel, and that is the knowledge of medicine and jurisprudence and what relates to the welfare of the body in this world.

And a kind that stands in the place of crossing the deserts and passing the steep ascents, and that is purifying the inner self from the impurities of qualities and climbing those lofty ascents which the earlier and later generations were unable to climb, except those granted success. This is travelling the path, and acquiring its knowledge is like acquiring knowledge of the directions of the road and its stages. And just as knowledge of the stages and desert routes is of no avail without travelling them, so too knowledge of refining character is of no avail without actually undertaking the refining; but the undertaking without knowledge is not possible.

And a third kind that stands in the place of the pilgrimage itself and its pillars, and that is knowledge of Allah Most High, His attributes, His angels, His acts, and all that we have mentioned in the headings of unveiling. Here lie salvation and the attainment of happiness. Salvation is gained by everyone who travels the path if his aim is the true goal, which is safety.

Know that this is the certainty of truth (haqq al-yaqin) according to the scholars firmly grounded in knowledge. I mean that they perceived it by an inner witnessing that is stronger and clearer than the seeing of eyes, and rose in it beyond the limit of imitation (taqlid) based on mere hearing. Their state is the state of one who was informed and believed, then witnessed and verified; and the state of others is that of one who accepted through good affirmation and faith but did not obtain witnessing and direct sight.

So happiness lies beyond the knowledge of unveiling ('ilm al-mukashafa), and the knowledge of unveiling lies beyond the knowledge of conduct ('ilm al-mu'amala), which is travelling the path of the Hereafter and crossing the steep ascents of the qualities.

And travelling the path of erasing blameworthy qualities lies beyond the knowledge of the qualities, and the knowledge of the path of treatment and of how to travel in it lies beyond the knowledge of the body's soundness and of the means that assist health.

The body's soundness comes through gathering together, mutual support, and cooperation, by which clothing, food, and shelter are obtained, and this is entrusted to the ruler, while its law, in keeping people on the course of justice and governance, is in the charge of the jurist.

As for the means of health, they are in the charge of the physician. And whoever said "Knowledge is of two kinds: the knowledge of bodies and the knowledge of religions," and alluded by it to jurisprudence, meant by it the apparent, widespread sciences, not the rare inner sciences.

If you say, "Why did you liken the knowledge of medicine and jurisprudence to preparing provisions and mount?", know that the one who strives toward Allah Most High to attain His nearness is the heart, not the body. By the heart I do not mean the perceptible piece of flesh; rather it is one of the secrets of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which the senses do not perceive, and a subtle essence (latifa) among His subtle things. At times it is called the spirit, and at times the tranquil self. The Law calls it the heart because it is the first mount for that secret, and by its means the whole body has become a mount and an instrument for that subtle essence. The lifting of the veil from that secret belongs to the knowledge of unveiling, and it is withheld; indeed, there is no licence to mention it. The most that is permitted is to say that it is a precious jewel and a rare pearl, nobler than these visible bodies, and it is only a divine command, as Allah Most High says, ⟦QS 17:85⟧ All created things are attributed to Allah Most High, but its attribution is nobler than the attribution of the rest of the body's organs. So both creation and command belong to Allah, and command is higher than creation.
The point is that this subtle essence is the one that strives toward nearness to the Lord, because it belongs to the command of the Lord; from Him is its source, and to Him

is its return. As for the body, it is its mount, which it rides and by means of which it strives. So for it the body on the path of Allah Most High is like the she-camel for the body on the path of the pilgrimage, and like the waterskin that stores the water the body needs. So every science whose aim is the welfare of the body belongs to the welfare of the mount.

And it is not hidden that medicine is likewise, for it is needed to preserve health for the body, and if a human being were alone he would need it. Jurisprudence differs from it in that, if a human being were alone, he might perhaps do without it. But he was created in such a way that he cannot live alone, since he cannot manage on his own to secure his food through ploughing, sowing, baking, and cooking, and to secure clothing and shelter, and to prepare the tools for all of that; so he was compelled to mix with others and to seek help.

Whenever people mix and their appetites are stirred, they pull against one another over the means of the appetites, quarrel, and fight, and their destruction results from their fighting, because of rivalry from outside, just as their destruction results from the opposition of the humours inside. By medicine, balance is preserved among the contending humours inside; by governance and justice, balance is preserved in rivalry from outside. The knowledge of the way to balance the humours is medicine, and the knowledge of the way to balance people's conditions in transactions and actions is jurisprudence (fiqh).

All of that is for preserving the body, which is a mount. So one devoted solely to the knowledge of jurisprudence or medicine, if he does not struggle against his self and does not set his heart right, is like one devoted solely to buying the she-camel and feeding it, and buying the waterskin and stitching it, if he does not travel the desert of the pilgrimage.

And one who spends his whole life in the finer points of expressions that arise in the disputations of jurisprudence is like one who spends his whole life in the finer points of the means by which the threads used to stitch the waterskin for the pilgrimage are made firm.

The ratio of these people to those who travel the path of setting the heart right, which leads to the knowledge of unveiling, is like the ratio of those others to those who travel the path of the pilgrimage or engage in its pillars. So reflect on this first, and accept advice free of charge from one to whom this has mostly come at a cost, and who reached it only after strenuous effort and complete boldness in parting from people, common and elite alike, by giving up imitation of them, which rests on mere appetite. This much is sufficient on the duties of the learner.
